transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Good morning. Thanks for coming in to see us here at the agency, Joe. I'm one of the agency representatives, and my name's Sally Baker.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Hi Sally. I think we spoke on the phone, didn't we?

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: That's right, we did. So thank you for sending in your CV. We've had quite a careful look at it and I think we have two jobs that might be suitable for you.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: The first one is in a company based in North London. They're looking for an administrative assistant.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: OK. What sort of company is it?

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: They're called Home Solutions and they design and make <q id="1">furniture.</q>

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Oh, I don't know much about that, but it sounds interesting.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Yes, well as I said, they want someone in their office, and looking at your past experience it does look as if you fit quite a few of the requirements. So on your CV it appears you've done some data entry?

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: So that's one skill they want. Then they expect the person they appoint to attend <q id="2">meetings</q> and take notes there …

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: OK. I've done that before, yes.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: And you'd need to be able to cope with general admin.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Filing, and keeping records and so on? That should be OK. And in my last job I also had to manage the <q id="3">diary.</q>

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Excellent. That's something they want here too. I'd suggest you add it to your CV – I don't think you mentioned that, did you?

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: So as far as the requirements go, they want good computer skills, of course, and they particularly mention spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: That should be fine.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: And interpersonal skills – which would be something they'd check with your references.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: I think that should be OK, yes.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Then they mention that they want someone who is careful and takes care with <q id="4">details</q> – just looking at your CV, I'd say you're probably alright there.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: I think so, yes. Do they want any special experience?

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: I think they wanted some experience of teleconferencing.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: I've got three years' experience of that.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Let's see, yes, good. In fact they're only asking for <q id="5">at least one year,</q> so that's great. So is that something that might interest you?

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: It is, yes. The only thing is, you said they were in North London so it would be quite a long commute for me.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: So the second position might suit you better as far as the location goes; that's for a warehouse assistant and that's in South London.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Yes, that would be a lot closer.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: And you've worked in a warehouse before, haven't you?

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: So as far as the responsibilities for this position go, they want someone who can manage the stock, obviously, and also <q id="6">deliveries.</q>

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: That should be OK. You've got to keep track of stuff, but I've always been quite good with numbers.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Good. That's their first requirement. And they want someone who's computer literate, which we know you are.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Then they mention organisational skills. They want someone who's well organised.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Yes, I think I am.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: And <q id="7">tidy?</q>

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Yes, they go together really, don't they?

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Sure. Then the usual stuff; they want someone who can communicate well both orally and in writing.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: OK. And for the last warehouse job I had, one of the things I enjoyed most was being part of a <q id="8">team.</q> I found that was really essential for the job.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Excellent. Yes, they do mention that they want someone who's used to that, yes. Now when you were working in a warehouse last time, what sorts of items were you dealing with?

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: It was mostly bathroom and kitchen equipment, sinks and stoves and fridges.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: So you're OK moving <q id="9">heavy</q> things?

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Sure. I'm quite strong, and I've had the training.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: Good. Now as far as experience goes, they mention they want someone with a licence, and that you have experience of driving in London – so you can cope with the traffic and so on.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Yes, no problem.

transcript.speaker: SALLY
transcript.text: And you've got experience of warehouse work … and the final thing they mention is <q id="10">customer service.</q> I think looking at your CV you're OK there.

transcript.speaker: JOE
transcript.text: Right. So what about pay? Can you tell me a bit more about that, please …

transcript.speaker: PRESENTER
transcript.text: My guest on the show today is Alice Riches who started the Street Play Scheme where she lives in Beechwood Road. For those of you that don't already know – Street Play involves local residents closing off their street for a few hours so that children have a chance to play in the street safely. She started it in her own street, Beechwood Road, and the idea caught on, and there are now Street Play Schemes all over the city. So when did you actually start the scheme, Alice?

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: Well, I first had the idea when my oldest child was still a toddler, so that's about six years ago now – but it took at least two years of campaigning before we were actually able to make it happen. <q id="11">So the scheme's been up and running for three years now.</q> We'd love to be able to close our road for longer – for the whole weekend, from Saturday morning until Sunday evening, for example. <q id="12">At the moment it's just once a week.</q> But when we started it was only once a month. But we're working on it.

transcript.speaker: PRESENTER
transcript.text: So what actually happens when Beechwood Road is closed?

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: <q id="13">We have volunteer wardens, mostly parents but some elderly residents too, who block off our road at either end.</q> The council have provided special signs but there's always a volunteer there to explain what's happening to any motorists. Generally, they're fine about it – we've only had to get the police involved once or twice.

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: Now I should explain that the road isn't completely closed to cars. But only residents' cars are allowed. If people really need to get in or out of Beechwood Road, it's not a problem – <q id="14">as long as they drive at under 20 kilometres per hour.</q> But most people just decide not to use their cars during this time, or they park in another street. The wardens are only there to stop through traffic.

transcript.speaker: PRESENTER
transcript.text: So can anyone apply to get involved in Street Play?

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: Absolutely – we want to include all kids <q id="15">in the city – especially those who live on busy roads.</q> It's here that demand is greatest. Obviously, there isn't such a demand in wealthier areas where the children have access to parks or large gardens – or in the suburbs where there are usually more places for children to play outside.

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: I'd recommend that anyone listening who likes the idea should just give it a go. We've been surprised by the positive reaction of residents all over the city. And that's not just parents. There are always a few who complain but they're a tiny minority. On the whole everyone is very supportive and say <q id="16">they're very happy to see children out on the street</q> – even if it does get quite noisy.

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: There have been so many benefits of Street Play for the kids. Parents really like the fact that the kids are getting fresh air instead of sitting staring at a computer screen, even if they're not doing anything particularly energetic. And of course it's great that kids can play with their friends outside without being supervised by their parents – but for me the biggest advantage is that kids <q id="17">develop confidence in themselves to be outside without their parents.</q> The other really fantastic thing is that children <q id="18">get to know the adults in the street – it's like having a big extended family.</q>

transcript.speaker: PRESENTER
transcript.text: It certainly does have a lot of benefits. I want to move on now and ask you about a related project in King Street.

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: Right. Well this was an experiment I was involved in where local residents decided to try and reduce the traffic along King Street, which is the busiest main road in our area, by persuading people not to use their cars for one day. We thought about making people pay more for parking – but we decided that would be really unpopular – so instead we just stopped people from parking on King Street but left the other car parks open.

transcript.speaker: ALICE
transcript.text: It was surprising how much of a difference all this made. As we'd predicted, air quality was significantly better but what I hadn't expected was <q id="19">how much quieter it would be</q> – even with the buses still running. Of course everyone said they felt safer but we were actually amazed that <q id="20">sales in the shops went up considerably that day</q> – we thought there'd be fewer people out shopping – not more.

transcript.speaker: PRESENTER
transcript.text: That's really interesting so the fact that …

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: Tom, could I ask you for some advice, please?

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Yes of course, if you think I can help. What's it about?

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: It's my first media studies assignment, and I'm not sure how to go about it. You must have done it last year.

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Is that the one comparing the coverage of a particular story in a range of newspapers?

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Oh yes, I really enjoyed writing it.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: So what sort of things do I need to compare?

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Well, there are several things. For example, there's the question of which <q id="21">page</q> of the newspaper the item appears on.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: You mean, because there's a big difference between having it on the front page and the bottom of page ten, for instance?

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Exactly. And that shows how important the editor thinks the story is. Then there's the <q id="22">size</q> – how many column inches the story is given, how many columns it spreads over.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: And I suppose that includes the headline.

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: It certainly does. It's all part of attracting the reader's attention.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: What about <q id="23">graphics</q> – whether there's anything visual in addition to the text?

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Yes, you need to consider those, too, because they can have a big effect on the reader's understanding of the story – sometimes a bigger effect than the text itself. Then you'll need to look at how the item is put together: what <q id="24">structure</q> is it given? Bear in mind that not many people read beyond the first paragraph, so what has the journalist put at the beginning? And if, say, there are conflicting opinions about something, does one appear near the end, where people probably won't read it?

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: And newspapers sometimes give wrong or misleading information, don't they? Either deliberately or by accident. Should I be looking at that, too?

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Yes, if you can. Compare what's in different versions, and as far as possible, try and work out what's true and what isn't. And that relates to a very important point: what's the writer's <q id="25">purpose,</q> or at least the most important one, if they have several. It may seem to be to inform the public, but often it's that they want to create fear, or controversy, or to make somebody look ridiculous.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: Gosh, I see what you mean. And I suppose the writer may make <q id="26">assumptions</q> about the reader.

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: That's right – about their knowledge of the subject, their attitudes, and their level of education, which means writing so that the readers understand without feeling patronised. All of that will make a difference to how the story is presented.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: Does it matter what type of story I write about?

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: No – national or international politics, the arts … Anything, as long as it's covered in two or three newspapers. Though of course it'll be easier and more fun if it's something you're interested in and know something about.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: And on that basis <q id="27">a national news item would be worth analysing – I'm quite keen on politics,</q> so I'll try and find a suitable topic. What did you choose for your analysis, Tom?

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: I was interested in how newspapers express their opinions explicitly, so <q id="28">I wanted to compare editorials in different papers, but when I started looking, I couldn't find two on the same topic</q> that I felt like analysing.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: In that case, <q id="28">I won't even bother to look.</q>

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: So in the end I chose a human interest story – a terribly emotional story about a young girl who was very ill, and lots of other people – mostly strangers – raised money so she could go abroad for treatment. Actually, I was surprised – some papers just wrote about how wonderful everyone was, but others considered the broader picture, like why treatment wasn't available here.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: <q id="29">I usually find stories like that raise quite strong feelings in me! I'll avoid that. Perhaps I'll choose an arts topic,</q> like different reviews of a film, or <q id="30">something about funding for the arts – I'll think about that.</q>

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: Yes, that might be interesting.

transcript.speaker: HAZEL
transcript.text: OK, well thanks a lot for your help, Tom. It's been really useful.

transcript.speaker: TOM
transcript.text: You're welcome. Good luck with the assignment, Hazel.
Nowadays, we use different products for personal cleanliness, laundry, dishwashing and household cleaning, but this is very much a 20th-century development.

The origins of cleanliness date back to prehistoric times. Since water is essential for life, the earliest people lived near water and knew something about its cleansing properties – at least <q id="31">that it rinsed mud off</q> their hands.

During the excavation of ancient Babylon, evidence was found that soapmaking was known as early as 2800 BC. Archaeologists discovered <q id="32">cylinders made of clay,</q> with inscriptions on them saying that fats were boiled with ashes. This is a method of making soap, though there's no reference to the purpose of this material.

The early Greeks bathed for aesthetic reasons and apparently didn't use soap. Instead, they cleaned their bodies with blocks of sand, pumice and ashes, then anointed themselves with oil, and scraped off the oil and dirt with <q id="33">a metal instrument known as a strigil.</q> They also used oil mixed with ashes. Clothes were washed without soap in streams.

The ancient Germans and Gauls are also credited with discovering how to make a substance called 'soap', made of melted animal fat and ashes. They <q id="34">used this mixture to tint their hair red.</q>

Soap got its name, according to an ancient Roman legend, from Mount Sapo, where animals were sacrificed, leaving deposits of animal fat. Rain washed these deposits, along with wood ashes, down into the clay soil along the River Tiber. Women found that this mixture greatly reduced the effort required to wash their clothes.

As Roman civilisation advanced, so did bathing. The first of <q id="35">the famous Roman baths, supplied with water from their aqueducts,</q> was built around 312 BC. The baths were luxurious, and bathing became very popular. And by the second century AD, the Greek physician Galen recommended soap for both medicinal and cleansing purposes.

After the fall of Rome in 467 AD and the resulting decline in bathing habits, much of Europe felt the impact of filth on public health. <q id="36">This lack of personal cleanliness and related unsanitary living conditions were major factors in the outbreaks of disease</q> in the Middle Ages, and especially the Black Death of the 14th century.

Nevertheless, soapmaking became an established craft in Europe, and associations of soapmakers guarded their trade secrets closely. Vegetable and animal oils were used with ashes of plants, along with <q id="37">perfume, apparently for the first time.</q> Gradually more varieties of soap became available for shaving and shampooing, as well as bathing and laundering.

A major step toward large-scale commercial soapmaking occurred in 1791, when a French chemist, Nicholas Leblanc, patented a process for <q id="38">turning salt into soda ash,</q> or sodium carbonate. Soda ash is the alkali obtained from ashes that combines with fat to form soap. The Leblanc process yielded quantities of good-quality, inexpensive soda ash.

Modern soapmaking was born some 20 years later, in the early 19th century, with the discovery by Michel Eugène Chevreul, another French chemist, of the chemical nature and relationship of fats, glycerine and fatty acids. His studies <q id="39">established the basis for both fat and soap chemistry, and soapmaking became a science.</q> Further developments during the 19th century made it easier and cheaper to manufacture soap.

Until the 19th century, soap was regarded as a luxury item, and was heavily taxed in several countries. As it became more readily available, it became an everyday necessity, a development that was reinforced <q id="40">when the high tax was removed.</q> Soap was then something ordinary people could afford, and cleanliness standards improved.
With this widespread use came the development of milder soaps for bathing and soaps for use in the washing machines that were available to consumers by the turn of the 20th century.
